body:
> v4.7.dev1 worked fine
> v4.7.dev2.official [[778cf54](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/778cf54dabd8a9e25b698a87036ab8604183f303)] broken

Are you sure about this?

I can reproduce the issue in both 4.7.dev1 and 4.7.dev2. I confirm that the MRP works fine in 4.6.1.stable.

> I can reproduce the issue in both 4.7.dev1 and 4.7.dev2.

Indeed it is reproducible in 4.7.dev1 too, that's a regression from #113228.

This is the same issue as #116375, which was closed by @dalexeev with a claim: [_"This is not a bug. The previous behavior was a bug"_](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/116375#issuecomment-3919522260).

But note the same exact issue was raised in the early 4.0: #62857, and back then it resulted in #72398 which allowed `points[1].x = 30` etc. syntax.

So it was working like that since 4.0; from the user point of view I consider this to be a big compatibility breakage.

#62857 is from an early 4.0. At the time, we probably weren't clear enough about how packed arrays should behave. In 3.x, pool arrays are pass-by-value types, and it has its own issues (which is why we made them pass-by-reference within `Variant`). There's also the fact that built-in property getters typically return a new array/dictionary each time when accessed.

In my opinion, the change in #113228 isn't a regression, but a bug fix. But yes, it breaks behavior that can be convenient and intuitive for users. However, it makes the language behavior more consistent within the current model:

1. If we consider packed arrays to be reference types, then their behavior for subscript chains shouldn't differ from that of other reference types (`Array`, `Dictionary`, `Object`). You can find an example in my PR.
2. The documentation for every built-in property of the `Packed*Array` type literally states that changing inplace will not work. This warning was added several minor versions before my PR. The fact that it worked in some exceptional cases is an inconsistency and a bug.

In my opinion, we should just mention this as a breaking change in the 4.7 migration guide. It's impossible to fix bugs in the engine without changing behavior. And unfortunately, not all behaviors can be clearly identified as buggy. Sometimes the bug is the inconsistency.

Yes, we're breaking someone's code that relied on this behavior. But we're eliminating the inconsistency (with `Array`/`Dictionary` and with the behavior of packed arrays themselves in other situations) and preventing surprise and debugging for future code (for example, when a user changes a property type from `PackedStringArray` to `Array[String]` or vice versa, and something breaks due to the difference in subscript chain behavior).

> In my opinion, we should just mention this as a breaking change in the 4.7 migration guide.

I'd say that's a minimum if we go with the current state. Note that even when aware about this breakage it's still not straightforward to find and fix these. I think in the current state the code like in the MRP should produce a warning. It's modifying a temporary which is pointless (unless the setter has some strange external/static side effects). With warnings users could at least easily hunt them down when migrating.

```gdscript
extends Line2D

func _ready():
	print("Before: ", points[1].x) # prints 0,0
	points[1].x = 30 # Fine-ish if produces a warning.
	print("After: ", points[1].x) # prints 0,0
```

> think in the current state the code like in the MRP should produce a warning. It's modifying a temporary which is pointless (unless the setter has some strange external/static side effects).

I'll take a look if you think it's worth it and could at least partially prevent confusion. However:

1. We can probably only implement such a warning for built-in properties. Detecting modification of a temporary created on the fly is generally quite difficult due to weak static analysis of side effects and control flow in GDScript.
2. Also, false negatives are possible in an untyped context. For example, `$Line2D.points[1].x = 30` won't produce the warning because `$Line2D` is of type `Node`, and therefore GDScript doesn't know what the `points` property is.

> > v4.7.dev1 worked fine
> > v4.7.dev2.official [[778cf54](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/778cf54dabd8a9e25b698a87036ab8604183f303)] broken
> 
> Are you sure about this?
> 
> I can reproduce the issue in both 4.7.dev1 and 4.7.dev2. I confirm that the MRP works fine in 4.6.1.stable.

Sorry, yes, 4.6.1.

But if this gets "fixed", how am I going to manipulate the points of my Line2D 😆 Removing the ability to manipulate points in such a way would just turn Line2D into dead objects. I'll have to go back to 4.6 stable I guess.

Anyway, elsewhere in the project I manipulate points of both a Polygon2D and a Line2D using an Animator (also in v4.7.dev2.official [778cf54da]), and there it works fine. So if I am not supposed to manipulate the coordinate points of a Line2D through code, it will be highly confusing if I can manipulate similar points through Animator and there it works but if I type the same thing in code then it doesn't.

(Edit: It's also confusing that punching in coordinates in the IDE while the build is running fails with a mystic "fieldwise_assign: Method/function failed. Returning: p_target", from the point of view of anyone using Godot, entering coordinates in Line2D.points is the same as changing any other property like size of a Node2D or changing text of a Button etc)

> But if this gets "fixed", how am I going to manipulate the points of my Line2D

You can modify a packed array in a temporary variable and assign it back to the built-in property:

```gdscript
var new_points := points
new_points[1].x = 30
points = new_points
```

That is, you first call the getter, then the setter. This is the main reason why this doesn't work as expected. Built-in properties are an illusion. You don't get direct access to the underlying data. Any built-in property is always a setter-getter pair.

Alternatively, you can use specialized methods `set_point_position()` and `get_point_position()`.

> You can modify a packed array in a temporary variable and assign it back to the built-in property:
> 
> var new_points := points
> new_points[1].x = 30
> points = new_points
> That is, you first call the getter, then the setter. This is the main reason why this doesn't work as expected. Built-in properties are an illusion. You don't get direct access to the underlying data. Any built-in property is always a setter-getter pair.
> 
> Alternatively, you can use specialized methods `set_point_position()` and `get_point_position()`.

Not as convenient (edit: and not intuitive at all) as `points[1].x += 30`… but I just tried it and it works. Thank you, I'll update my project.

> I'll take a look if you think it's worth it and could at least partially prevent confusion.

Thanks! Can't tell if it's worth, as I'm not sure how much effort would it take. For sure it would help to lower the confusion, even if it wouldn't warn in all cases (as you've mentioned).

To be clear I'm not necessarily against the fix/breakage. But for the current state I would not be surprised if this or similar issue would end up needing to be pinned once 4.7 will be tested broader by the users (probably rc/stable stage). Preventing this by smoothening the migration process (e.g. by adding warnings) would be a "nice to have".

Following this logic, code like this shouldn't work:
```
var d # distance between the mouse and the current
d = points[0].distance_to(get_global_mouse_position())

```

In my project I changed it to
```
dP = get_point_position(0)
dM = get_global_mouse_position()
d = dP.distance_to(dM)
```
which I assume is the intended way of going about this.

> Following this logic, code like this shouldn't work:
> 
> ```
> var d # distance between the mouse and the current
> d = points[0].distance_to(get_global_mouse_position())
> ```

@inhalt120g Nothing has changed for local variables and custom class members without setters/getters. You access the packed array directly and modify its data. You don't need to use a temporary variable here.

The change only applies to custom class members with setters/getters (the setter is no longer called redundantly, to be consistent with arrays/dictionaries and method calls) and built-in properties (which are always bound using a setter and getter, plus packed arrays are passed by value within the engine, unlike `Variant` and GDScript).

Here's a GDScript equivalent of what happens when you access built-in properties. I used `Array` instead of `Packed*Array` so you can test it on previous versions (with the bug):

```gdscript
extends Node

var points: Array[Vector2]:
    set(value):
        points = value.duplicate()
    get:
        return points.duplicate()

func _ready() -> void:
    points = [Vector2.ZERO]
    points[0].x = 30
    print(points) # Prints `[(0.0, 0.0)]`.
```

Also note that even in previous versions, this (inconsistently) only works for assignment chains, not for method calls:

```gdscript
extends Line2D

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
    points.clear() # This line has no effect.
    points[1].x += 100 * delta # Why does it work then?!
```

I agree this is a good change for language consistency, and glad that a warning was added in #118002 (or I would have been bitten by this in a really subtle way in my game, so thanks).

It would be good to call this out as a breaking change in the 4.7 release notes. (I'm not sure what the process is for writing those release notes, if there is a draft already somewhere, but it would be great to remember to add this, as it does break naughty code that was not following the documentation 🤫.)
